units: a short cooking time is needed to get a firm bite
too much sauce softens a firm preparation
low, drawn-out heat loosens the fibers without drying them
patient sieving gives a smooth preparation that coats the palate
a smooth texture takes the edge off harsh flavors
liquid poured in cold makes lumps in a purée
flesh full of fibers points to a badly chosen cut
batter that is too wet gives a cake that sinks like a sponge
texture registers before taste does
text: Three textures rule the plate of a careful cook, and each answers to rules of its own. Crunch comes first. It calls for brief cooking, firm material and restrained seasoning, since a heavy sauce softens it at once. Melting texture takes second place, and it grows out of low, drawn-out heat that loosens the fibers without drying them. Smoothness closes the set. Patient sieving is what gives it that coat on the palate, and it rounds off flavors that would otherwise bite. Alongside those three families sit the accidents every cook dreads. A lumpy purée gives away liquid poured in cold. Stringy meat announces a badly chosen cut. A spongy cake tells of batter soaked with moisture. Knowing the faults is worth as much as mastering the successes, because texture registers before taste does.

units: talk about cooking shifted as households cooked less
the speed of a meal was prized first
the food industry claimed to free whoever prepared the meals
ready-made dishes were then blamed for having no taste
they were faulted for carrying too much salt
cooking shows put the work of the hands on display
what happened in home kitchens never matched that display
a recent line of talk weighs a plate by its price and its origin
each phase corrected the excess of the one before it
text: Public talk about cooking has changed shape as households drifted away from their own stoves. Speed was prized first of all. A meal had to fit inside a narrow slot, and the food industry promised to set whoever cooked entirely free. Then the mood turned, and the ready-made dishes were blamed for their flat taste, their overwhelming saltiness, their dreary sameness. Cooking programs answered by putting the work of the hands on display, though what went on in home kitchens never quite matched the picture. A third line of talk takes over now, weighing a plate by what it costs and by where it came from. Nothing about that sequence is absurd. Each stage trimmed back the excess of the one before it. One question stays open all the same, and nobody has settled it. Who is left with room enough to cook without pressure?

genre: portrait / biographie (personne désignée par son rôle)
units: the baker credits her skill to a childhood spent beside a family mill
she turned down flour blends mixed in advance
that refusal cost her customers early on
her dough ferments at its own pace
the slow fermentation thickens the crust
her bread gives off a faintly sharp smell that throws off newcomers
many disappointed customers come back because the bread keeps for a week
her batches are gone before the middle of the day
she puts her success down to stubbornness rather than to a gift
text: Ask the baker on the corner where that dense loaf of hers comes from, and she will tell you she had almost nothing to do with it herself. Her parents ran a mill, so she grew up with her hands in flour, and the habit settled everything that came after. Since she had told grains apart by touch from childhood on, she turned down the ready-mixed flours, and that cost her customers early on. Her dough rises at its own pace, so the crust thickens and the loaf carries a faintly sharp edge that throws off newcomers. Plenty of people walk out disappointed, then come back, because this bread keeps for a whole week. She has never needed a sign over the door. The batches are gone before midday, and the line of customers spills out onto the walkway. Her success, she laughs, rests on stubbornness, not on any gift.

units: this establishment listed more dishes than its kitchen could handle
the broth had no flavor at the first service
a heavy sauce buried a delicate fish
the chocolate dessert felt gritty in the mouth
the staff out front did their job properly
the manager cut half the dishes from the list
a cook hired from a country inn took over the long cooking
plates arrived hotter and the wait shrank from the following week
a short menu is presented here as the condition of sound cooking
text: The place that just opened at the end of the shopping street had a familiar trouble. Its menu ran far too long, and it listed preparations the kitchen could not handle. The opening service made that plain enough. The broth came out flat, a heavy sauce buried a delicate fish, and the chocolate dessert felt gritty under the spoon. Out front, the staff did their job well enough. The manager settled matters by cutting the list in half and by handing the long, slow cooking to a second cook hired away from a country inn. The difference showed within the following week. Plates left the kitchen hotter, waits grew shorter, and the evening shift stopped calling for extra hands. A short menu is no confession of poverty. Here it is the very condition under which a kitchen finally cooks the way it should.

units: the woman written to describes the kitchen she now has as nothing like the old one
the old kitchen smelled of damp wood and baked fruit
the recent one gives off a smell of metal and soap
the copper pan heated unevenly
the sauce had to be watched without a break
the recent burner answers the dial at once
the writer sees a trade in this rather than an improvement
the old soups had a cloudy color and a deep flavor
vegetables cooked in the recent kitchen keep some firmness
text: You write that the kitchen you now have is nothing like the one we used to share, and I think I follow you. Ours smelled of damp wood and baked apples. Yours, you say, smells of cold metal and soap. In ours the copper pan heated in patches, and a sauce had to be watched the way you watch a small child. In yours the burner answers the dial and nothing boils over. What I see there is less a step forward than a straight trade. You gained precision and you gave up the waiting. Our soups turned cloudy and tasted deep, and your bright kitchen will never reach anything like that. Yours, on the other hand, leave the vegetables a firmness we knew nothing about. Write and tell me what you cook in the evenings. I would like to picture the steam on your windows the way I still see it on ours.

units: whether an emulsion holds depends on three separate things
an egg yolk or some mustard wraps the droplets of fat
that wrapping keeps the droplets from running together
oil added little by little gives the binder time to work
a heavy splash of oil tears the preparation apart
very cold liquid sets part of the fat and makes a lumpy mass
a split sauce is rescued by starting from a fresh yolk in a clean bowl
the failed mixture is worked back in a little at a time
an emulsion that has held looks nearly clear at its rim
text: What separates an emulsion that holds together from one that splits apart? Three separate things govern it, and each can be examined on its own. The first is the binder. An egg yolk, or a dab of mustard, wraps every droplet of fat and keeps the droplets from running together. The second is the pace of the pouring. A thin thread of oil gives the binder the leisure to do its work, while a heavy splash tears the whole preparation apart. The third is temperature. Liquid straight out of the cold sets part of the fat and leaves a lumpy mass behind. So how do you rescue a sauce that has already split? Start over with a fresh yolk in a clean bowl, then work the failed mixture back in a little at a time. An emulsion that has held looks nearly clear at the rim and velvety in the middle.

units: the head waiter tells the young cook the dining room will be full
the cook says he put the garnishes together as soon as the doors opened
only the herbs are missing
the purchasing manager reports a late delivery
she suggests using a sharp condiment kept in a jar
the head waiter agrees on condition that the menu says so
a guest finds his dish too salty halfway through the evening
the cook owns the mistake and offers to make the plate again
in the end not one order was lost
text: At the start of service the head waiter reminded the young cook that every table in the room was booked. The cook answered that he had put the garnishes together as soon as the doors opened, and that only the herbs were still missing. The purchasing manager then reported that the delivery would run late, and she offered to stand in a sharp condiment kept in a jar for the fresh herbs. The head waiter hesitated, then agreed, on condition that the menu said so. Halfway through the evening a guest sent word that his dish tasted too salty. The cook owned the mistake at once and offered a fresh plate, which went out again with no real delay. As the night closed, the buyer summed things up for the gathered staff. Not one order had been lost, and everyone had been equal to the work in hand.

genre: texte historique de vulgarisation (sans époque nommée)
units: keeping food once rested on salt, smoke and sugar
those limits shaped tastes that lasted
salt pulls the water out of meat, which forced people to soak it before cooking
root vegetables went into broths to balance a flavor that pushed too hard
smoke left sharp compounds on the surface of the cuts
cooks rubbed those cuts with herbs and fat to soften that attack
sugar was kept for fruit because it was scarcer
mechanical cold made these techniques unnecessary
the techniques lived on as tastes people prefer
text: Long before mechanical cold ever reached the kitchen, keeping food meant salt, smoke and sugar. That single limit shaped whole tastes. Salt pulled the water out of meat, so the meat had to be soaked before it could be cooked, and broths filled up with root vegetables to balance a flavor that pushed far too hard. Smoke left sharp compounds on the outside of every cut, so cooks learned to rub the surface with herbs and fat and take that attack down. Sugar, being scarcer, was kept for fruit, whose flesh it turned clear and yielding. Once the icebox and then the cooling machine had spread through kitchens, none of this was needed any longer. It did not go away, though. By then these had become tastes that people actively looked for, and they cost more today than anything sold fresh.

units: sticky rice clumps into a pasty mass as it cooks
the main cause is not the pot you use
the grain lets go of starch the moment it heats in water
that starch works like glue
rinsing the grain until the water runs clear solves part of the trouble
measuring the water keeps the cooking from dragging on
cooking that drags on crushes the grains
cutting the heat before the end lets the steam finish the job
salting the water at the start fixes a taste that falls flat
text: Your rice clumps up into a pasty mass? It happens more often than anyone admits, and the pot is rarely responsible. The grain releases its starch the moment it heats in water, and that starch behaves exactly like glue. First fix: rinse the rice under cold water until the water runs clear, then leave it to drain. Second fix: measure the water instead of pouring it by eye, because too much drags the cooking out, and cooking that drags on crushes the grains. Third fix: cut the heat before the end you were told to wait for, put the lid on, and let the steam finish the job without any stirring at all. If the taste still falls flat, salt the water at the start rather than the plate at the end. What you end up with is separate grains, firm to the bite, ready to accept any sauce without disintegrating.

units: an oven breakdown upset a caterer's evening
the crew moved the whole menu onto fierce heat
the guests thus compared two ways of cooking without thinking about it
the root vegetables roasted the day before had a soft center and a sweet surface
the same vegetables seared in a pan kept a sharp firmness and a plain bitterness
the fish from the oven had loose, airy flesh
the fish cooked over the flame had brittle skin and denser flesh
the guests who were asked split into two camps of about equal size
the caterer now offers both ways of cooking
text: An oven that quit turned a caterer's evening into a demonstration that nobody had planned. With no dry heat left, the crew moved the whole menu onto fierce burners, and the guests ended up comparing two ways of cooking without once thinking about it. The day before, the same root vegetables had roasted without hurry. Their centers went soft, their surfaces turned sweet, their smell came out round. That night, seared in a pan, they held a sharp firmness and a plain bitterness much closer to the raw vegetable. The fish followed the same swing. Out of the oven its flesh was loose and slightly spongy. Over the flame the skin turned brittle and the inside sat denser. Asked on the way out, the guests fell into two camps of about equal size. The caterer took the lesson and now offers both.
